column1: What does the divergence of a field measure?
column2: Net outward flux per unit volume at a point: the density of sources (positive) or sinks (negative).

column1: What does the curl of a field measure?
column2: Circulation per unit area about each axis: how much the field swirls around a point, with direction by the right-hand rule.

column1: State the divergence theorem.
column2: ∮<sub>S</sub> A·dS = ∫<sub>v</sub> ∇·A dv: total outward flux through a closed surface equals the integrated divergence inside.

column1: State Stokes's theorem.
column2: ∮<sub>C</sub> A·dℓ = ∫<sub>S</sub> (∇×A)·dS: circulation around a loop equals the flux of the curl through any surface bounded by it.

column1: Scale factors (h<sub>1</sub>, h<sub>2</sub>, h<sub>3</sub>) for cylindrical and spherical coordinates?
column2: Cylindrical (1, ρ, 1); spherical (1, r, r sin θ).

column1: Divergence of a purely radial field A<sub>r</sub>(r) in spherical coordinates?
column2: (1/r²) d(r²A<sub>r</sub>)/dr. A field falling as 1/r² has zero divergence away from the origin.

column1: Which two vector identities make potentials possible?
column2: ∇×∇f = 0 (curl-free fields are gradients) and ∇·(∇×A) = 0 (divergence-free fields are curls).

column1: What is ∇²(1/r)?
column2: −4πδ³(r): zero everywhere except at the origin, where it is a spike whose volume integral is −4π.

column1: Boundary conditions on E and D at a dielectric interface?
column2: Tangential E continuous; normal D jumps by the free surface charge ρ<sub>s</sub> (continuous if there is none).

column1: Fields at the surface of a perfect conductor?
column2: E is normal to the surface with D<sub>n</sub> = ρ<sub>s</sub>; tangential E is zero; the field inside is zero.

column1: Poisson's and Laplace's equations?
column2: ∇²V = −ρ<sub>v</sub>/ε; Laplace's equation is the charge-free case ∇²V = 0.

column1: Why does the uniqueness theorem matter in practice?
column2: Any potential that satisfies Laplace's (or Poisson's) equation and the boundary conditions is the answer, however it was found (guess, image, series or grid).

column1: Image of a point charge q at height d above a grounded plane?
column2: A charge −q at depth d below it; valid only for the region above the plane. The force is q²/[4πε(2d)²], attractive.

column1: Capacitance per metre of a coaxial line?
column2: C′ = 2πε/ln(b/a).

column1: Where is the field largest in a coax, and how large?
column2: At the inner conductor: E<sub>max</sub> = V/[a ln(b/a)].

column1: Two dielectric layers between capacitor plates: which layer has the larger field?
column2: The one with the lower permittivity (D is continuous, so E = D/ε). Air voids in insulation therefore break down first.

column1: What does a finite-difference Laplace solver do?
column2: Replaces each grid node's potential by the average of its neighbours (the mean-value property), iterating until the boundaries' values settle the interior.

column1: Magnetostatic field equations?
column2: ∇·B = 0 and ∇×H = J; integral form: no net flux out of any closed surface, and ∮H·dℓ = I<sub>enc</sub> (Ampère).

column1: Field at the centre of a circular loop of radius a carrying I?
column2: B = μ<sub>0</sub>I/(2a).

column1: Field of a long straight wire?
column2: B = μ<sub>0</sub>I/(2πρ), circling the wire.

column1: Boundary conditions on B and H?
column2: Normal B continuous; tangential H jumps by the surface current K.

column1: Two definitions of inductance?
column2: Flux linkage per current, L = NΦ/I, or stored energy, L = 2W<sub>m</sub>/I².

column1: Reluctance of a magnetic path?
column2: ℛ = ℓ/(μA); NI = Φ Σℛ and L = N²/Σℛ, like resistors in series.

column1: Why do power inductors have air gaps?
column2: The gap holds most of the reluctance and the stored energy, so the core stores energy without saturating and L depends on a dimension, not on the core's variable permeability.

column1: External inductance per metre of a coax?
column2: L′ = (μ/2π) ln(b/a); with C′ = 2πε/ln(b/a), L′C′ = με.

column1: Why does a loop's area matter for board layout?
column2: Inductance (and pickup of external fields) grows with loop area, so signals should return directly beneath their own trace.

column1: Faraday's law in differential form?
column2: ∇×E = −∂B/∂t: a changing magnetic field produces a circulating electric field.

column1: What is the displacement current, and why is it needed?
column2: ∂D/∂t; without it Ampère's law contradicts charge conservation (e.g. across a charging capacitor), and with it the equations predict waves.

column1: Write Maxwell's equations in phasor form.
column2: ∇×E = −jωμH; ∇×H = (σ + jωε)E; ∇·D = ρ<sub>v</sub>; ∇·B = 0.

column1: When does a material behave as a conductor rather than a dielectric?
column2: When σ/(ωε) ≫ 1 (conduction current dominates); ≪ 1 means a good dielectric. The same material can be either, depending on frequency.

column1: Charge relaxation time?
column2: τ = ε/σ: the time for free charge inside a conductor to decay by 1/e. The ratio σ/ωε equals 1/(ωτ).

column1: Poynting vector and its time average with peak phasors?
column2: S = E×H, the power flux density (W/m²); time average ½Re(E×H*).

column1: When is a lumped circuit model good enough?
column2: When the structure is much smaller than a wavelength (≲ λ/10), or its delay is much shorter than the signal's rise time.

column1: Speed and intrinsic impedance of a plane wave in a lossless medium?
column2: v<sub>p</sub> = 1/√(με) = c/n and η = √(μ/ε) = η<sub>0</sub>/n, with η<sub>0</sub> ≈ 376.7 Ω.

column1: How are E, H and the propagation direction related in a plane wave?
column2: They are mutually perpendicular, H = k̂×E/η, and E×H points along the direction of travel.

column1: Propagation constant of a general medium?
column2: γ = α + jβ = √(jωμ(σ + jωε)); fields vary as e<sup>−γz</sup>.

column1: Skin depth of a good conductor?
column2: δ = 1/√(πfμσ); fields and current fall by 1/e per δ (8.686 dB).

column1: Copper's skin depth at 60 Hz, 1 MHz and 1 GHz?
column2: About 8.5 mm, 66 µm and 2.1 µm.

column1: Surface resistance?
column2: R<sub>s</sub> = 1/(σδ) = √(πfμ/σ), rising as √f; the wall behaves like a sheet one skin depth thick.

column1: AC resistance of a round wire much thicker than δ?
column2: R<sub>s</sub>/(2πa) per metre, about a/(2δ) times the DC value.

column1: Wavelength inside a good conductor?
column2: 2πδ, so over one wavelength inside the metal the field falls by e<sup>−2π</sup>, about 55 dB: the wave barely travels.

column1: Why do submarines use very low frequencies?
column2: Seawater (σ ≈ 4 S/m) has a skin depth of only 1–3 m from about 10 to 40 kHz and much less above, so only the lowest frequencies reach useful depths.

column1: Phase velocity versus group velocity?
column2: v<sub>p</sub> = ω/β is the speed of a single frequency's phase; v<sub>g</sub> = dω/dβ is the speed of energy and signals. They differ in a dispersive medium.

column1: Circular polarization?
column2: Two equal orthogonal components 90° apart in phase; the field vector rotates once per cycle. Its handedness is defined relative to the direction of travel.

column1: Reflection coefficient at normal incidence?
column2: Γ = (η<sub>2</sub> − η<sub>1</sub>)/(η<sub>2</sub> + η<sub>1</sub>); τ = 1 + Γ.

column1: Air-to-glass (n = 1.5) reflectance at normal incidence?
Quarter-wave antireflection coating?
column2: Index √(n<sub>0</sub>n<sub>s</sub>) and thickness λ<sub>0</sub>/(4n<sub>1</sub>): the two reflections cancel at the design wavelength.

column1: Snell's law?
column2: n<sub>1</sub> sin θ<sub>i</sub> = n<sub>2</sub> sin θ<sub>t</sub>: the tangential wavenumber is continuous across the boundary.

column1: Critical angle?
column2: sin θ<sub>c</sub> = n<sub>2</sub>/n<sub>1</sub> for n<sub>1</sub> > n<sub>2</sub>; beyond it all power reflects and an evanescent field decays in the second medium.

column1: Brewster angle?
column2: tan θ<sub>B</sub> = n<sub>2</sub>/n<sub>1</sub>; parallel (TM) polarization is transmitted with no reflection. Glare from water is therefore mostly s-polarized.

column1: How does a metal sheet several skin depths thick shield a plane wave?
column2: By reflection (impedance mismatch, about 20 log[η<sub>0</sub>/4|η<sub>c</sub>|]) plus absorption (8.686 dB per skin depth of thickness).

column1: Telegrapher's equations (lossless)?
column2: ∂v/∂z = −L′ ∂i/∂t and ∂i/∂z = −C′ ∂v/∂t; Z<sub>0</sub> = √(L′/C′), v<sub>p</sub> = 1/√(L′C′).

column1: Voltage launched onto a line by a source V<sub>s</sub> with resistance R<sub>s</sub>?
column2: v<sup>+</sup> = V<sub>s</sub>Z<sub>0</sub>/(R<sub>s</sub> + Z<sub>0</sub>): the line looks like Z<sub>0</sub> until reflections return.

column1: Reflection coefficient at an open and at a short?
column2: +1 (voltage doubles) and −1 (voltage cancels).

column1: What is a bounce diagram?
column2: A space–time plot of each reflected wave; each round trip multiplies the wave by Γ<sub>L</sub>Γ<sub>S</sub>, and the load voltage converges to the DC divider value.

column1: When is a PCB trace a transmission line?
column2: When its one-way delay exceeds about one-sixth of the signal's rise time (rules from one-quarter to one-tenth are used); the real threshold depends on driver impedance and noise budget.

column1: What does a capacitive load do to a step on a line?
column2: Starts as a short (Γ = −1) and ends as an open; the load voltage rises as 2v<sup>+</sup>(1 − e<sup>−t/Z₀C</sup>), slowing the edge.

column1: Series versus parallel (end) termination?
column2: Series: R<sub>s</sub> = Z<sub>0</sub> at the source, half-amplitude wave doubles at an open end, no DC power. Parallel: R<sub>L</sub> = Z<sub>0</sub> at the end, no reflections anywhere, but DC current.

column1: What does a TDR measure?
column2: Reflections of a fast step versus time: distance = v<sub>p</sub>t/2, impedance from the reflected step's size, L or C from its shape.

column1: Input impedance of a lossless line?
column2: Z<sub>in</sub> = Z<sub>0</sub>(Z<sub>L</sub> + jZ<sub>0</sub> tan βℓ)/(Z<sub>0</sub> + jZ<sub>L</sub> tan βℓ).

column1: What do λ/2 and λ/4 lines do to a load?
column2: λ/2 repeats Z<sub>L</sub>; λ/4 inverts it to Z<sub>0</sub>²/Z<sub>L</sub>.

column1: Input impedance of short- and open-circuited stubs?
column2: Short: jZ<sub>0</sub> tan βℓ (a short one is an inductor). Open: −jZ<sub>0</sub> cot βℓ (a short one is a capacitor ≈ C′ℓ).

column1: VSWR in terms of Γ?
column2: (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|): the ratio of maximum to minimum voltage along the line.

column1: Return loss and mismatch loss?
column2: RL = −20 log|Γ|; ML = −10 log(1 − |Γ|²), the power not delivered because of reflection.

column1: Where are the voltage maxima and minima on a mismatched line?
column2: Max where Γ(d) = Γ<sub>L</sub>e<sup>−j2βd</sup> is real and positive, min a quarter-wavelength away; they repeat every λ/2.

column1: Quarter-wave transformer impedance?
column2: Z<sub>1</sub> = √(Z<sub>0</sub>R<sub>L</sub>), exact only at the design frequency.

column1: Low-loss attenuation constant of a line?
column2: α ≈ R′/(2Z<sub>0</sub>) + G′Z<sub>0</sub>/2: conductor loss rises as √f (skin effect), dielectric loss as f.

column1: Condition for a distortionless line?
column2: R′/L′ = G′/C′: α and v<sub>p</sub> become independent of frequency.

column1: What is the Smith chart?
column2: The Γ plane with circles of constant normalized resistance and reactance drawn on it; moving along a lossless line rotates Γ about the centre, once per λ/2.

column1: Normalized impedance from Γ?
column2: z = (1 + Γ)/(1 − Γ); the chart's centre is a perfect match (Γ = 0).

column1: Q and component values of an L-network?
column2: Q = √(R<sub>high</sub>/R<sub>low</sub> − 1); series X = QR<sub>low</sub>, shunt B = Q/R<sub>high</sub>.

column1: Why do larger impedance ratios give narrower matches?
column2: A larger step needs a higher Q, and the reactances drift off the match faster with frequency.

column1: How does a single-stub match work?
column2: Move along the line until the admittance's real part equals 1/Z<sub>0</sub>, then cancel the susceptance with a short or open stub.

column1: What does the Bode–Fano limit say?
column2: For a parallel RC load, ∫ln(1/|Γ|)dω ≤ π/(RC): no lossless network can match it well over an arbitrarily wide band.

column1: Conjugate match versus noise match?
column2: Conjugate (Z<sub>S</sub> = Z<sub>L</sub>*) maximizes power transfer; a low-noise amplifier is matched to its noise-optimal source impedance, which is generally different.

column1: TE<sub>10</sub> cutoff of a rectangular guide?
column2: f<sub>c</sub> = c/(2a): half a wavelength must fit across the broad wall.

column1: Single-mode band of a standard guide with b = a/2?
column2: From c/(2a) to c/a, where TE<sub>20</sub> and TE<sub>01</sub> start.

column1: Phase constant and guide wavelength above cutoff?
column2: β = k√(1 − (f<sub>c</sub>/f)²); λ<sub>g</sub> = λ/√(1 − (f<sub>c</sub>/f)²), longer than in free space.

column1: Phase and group velocity in a waveguide?
column2: v<sub>p</sub> > c and v<sub>g</sub> < c with v<sub>p</sub>v<sub>g</sub> = c²; v<sub>g</sub> → 0 at cutoff.

column1: TE wave impedance?
column2: η/√(1 − (f<sub>c</sub>/f)²): larger than η, infinite at cutoff.

column1: What happens below cutoff?
column2: The field decays as e<sup>−αz</sup> with α ≈ k<sub>c</sub> = π/a (TE<sub>10</sub>) well below cutoff: the principle of a microwave oven's door holes, together with the weak coupling of small apertures.

column1: Resonant frequencies of a rectangular cavity?
column2: f = (c/2)√((m/a)² + (n/b)² + (ℓ/d)²); TE<sub>101</sub> is lowest when b is the smallest side.

column1: Quality factor of a cavity?
column2: Q = ω<sub>0</sub>W/P<sub>loss</sub>; roughly volume/(surface × skin depth), thousands for copper at X band.

column1: Loaded Q at critical coupling?
column2: Q<sub>L</sub> = Q<sub>0</sub>/2 (external loss equals internal loss), so the bandwidth doubles.

column1: Numerical aperture and V-number of a step-index fibre?
column2: NA = √(n<sub>1</sub>² − n<sub>2</sub>²); V = (2πa/λ)NA.

column1: Single-mode condition for a step-index fibre?
column2: V < 2.405 (the first zero of J<sub>0</sub>).

column1: Why is multimode fibre limited to short links?
column2: Its many modes travel at different speeds (modal dispersion), smearing pulses over distance.

column1: Radiation resistance of a short dipole with uniform current?
column2: (2πη<sub>0</sub>/3)(ℓ/λ)² ≈ 789(ℓ/λ)² Ω; a centre-fed short dipole with triangular current has a quarter of this.

column1: Directivity of a short dipole and a half-wave dipole?
Radiation resistance of a half-wave dipole?
column2: About 73 Ω (plus about j42 Ω of reactance unless shortened slightly).

column1: Gain versus directivity?
column2: G = e<sub>r</sub>D with radiation efficiency e<sub>r</sub> = R<sub>rad</sub>/(R<sub>rad</sub> + R<sub>loss</sub>).

column1: Effective aperture and gain?
column2: A<sub>e</sub> = Gλ²/(4π).

column1: Friis transmission equation?
column2: P<sub>r</sub> = P<sub>t</sub>G<sub>t</sub>G<sub>r</sub>[λ/(4πR)]²; free-space path loss 20 log(4πR/λ) dB, +6 dB per doubling of distance.

column1: What is EIRP?
column2: Transmitted power times antenna gain (dBm + dBi): the power an isotropic antenna would need to give the same peak power density.

column1: Where does the far field begin for an aperture of size D?
column2: About 2D²/λ (and beyond a few wavelengths).

column1: Why is a phone's head exposure (below 6 GHz) assessed by SAR rather than power density?
column2: The head is in the antenna's reactive near field (r ≲ λ/2π), where far-field power density is meaningless; absorbed power per mass is what heats tissue.

column1: Array factor of N equally spaced elements?
column2: |sin(Nψ/2)/sin(ψ/2)| with ψ = kd sin θ + β; the pattern is element pattern × array factor.

column1: How is a phased array steered?
column2: Progressive phase β = −kd sin θ<sub>0</sub> between neighbours points the beam to θ<sub>0</sub>.

column1: Condition for no grating lobes when scanning to θ<sub>max</sub>?
column2: Element spacing d < λ/(1 + |sin θ<sub>max</sub>|); λ/2 spacing avoids them for every scan short of endfire.

column1: Why does an array's EIRP grow as N²?
column2: N elements give N times the power and, adding coherently, N times the gain: 6 dB per doubling.

column1: What happens to EIRP when a phased array scans off broadside?
column2: The element pattern falls (roughly as cos θ in power for a planar array), so EIRP drops by about 3 dB at 60°; the beam also widens.
